title: A Trip to the Moon
description: Méliès's 1902 A Trip to the Moon, loosely from Jules Verne, used stop motion and superimposition, reached audiences internationally and helped make story films mainstream.

facts.text: In A Trip to the Moon, Méliès used camera tricks such as stop motion and superimposition to create fantasy.

title: A genre promises the familiar and the new
description: A genre promises audiences something like what they enjoyed before, yet also something new; long familiarity trains viewers to expect its characters, music, lighting and plot devices.

facts.text: Britannica says genres promise audiences something similar to what they have enjoyed in the past, yet also something quite new and different.
Viewers largely knew what to expect from a genre film: they recognized its stars or characters and were sensitive to its music, lighting and plot devices from long familiarity.
Most genres are defined by subject matter or setting, such as the western, the gangster film, the police thriller and the science-fiction film.

title: Why studios loved genres
description: A studio making several films in one genre could reuse sets and costumes and keep the same personnel on it, building a routine that made filmmaking quicker and often better.

facts.text: A studio making half a dozen police thrillers in one year could save time and money by reusing sets, costumes and other items.
Studios could assign the same writers, directors, crews and actors to a genre, building a routine that often made filmmaking quicker and better.

title: The Western: America's own genre
description: Set in the American West of roughly the 1850s to 1900, the Western is basically an American creation; its pattern dates from 1903, Stagecoach revived it in 1939, and it later filled TV screens.

facts.text: The western is set in the American West, usually from the 1850s to the end of the 19th century.
Britannica calls the western basically an American creation, and the Library of Congress calls it a historically inspired genre invented in the United States.
Britannica dates the western film from The Great Train Robbery (1903), which set the pattern for many films that followed.
Cowboys, the town sheriff and the U.S. marshal are staple figures of the western, whose conflicts are often settled by violence and physical courage.
By 1939 the western had long been relegated to B-movie status; John Ford's Stagecoach, starring John Wayne, revitalized the genre with its critical and commercial success.
TV westerns such as Gunsmoke and Bonanza drew large audiences in the late 1950s and the 1960s.

title: How Westerns pictured Native Americans
description: Conflict between pioneers and Native Americans is a basic Western theme; early films showed Native Americans with little understanding, and later Westerns shifted sympathy toward them.

facts.text: Conflict between white pioneers and Native Americans is one of the western's basic themes, and earlier films showed Native Americans with remarkably little understanding or appreciation.
Later westerns shifted sympathy toward Native Americans, among them John Ford's Cheyenne Autumn (1964), Little Big Man (1970) and Dances with Wolves (1990).

title: Musicals sing what speech can't carry
description: A musical film integrates musical numbers into its plot; over the 1930s and 1940s plot and music grew more unified, until song and dance carried a film's key emotional moments.

facts.text: Britannica defines a musical film as a motion picture whose plot integrates musical numbers.
Fred Astaire's dances with Ginger Rogers at RKO, as in Top Hat (1935), worked as sophisticated statements of romantic love.
Late-1930s and 1940s musicals such as The Wizard of Oz (1939) showed a trend toward greater unification of plot and music.
In Singin' in the Rain (1952), song and dance rather than dialogue carry the important moments; Gene Kelly swings from a lamppost celebrating new love.

title: Berkeley's spectacle and Astaire's simplicity
description: Busby Berkeley filmed dancers from overhead in geometric patterns inside well-worn stories; by the mid-1930s dance teams led by Astaire, filmed in full figure with few cuts, took over.

facts.text: Busby Berkeley placed the camera directly above his performers to show them moving in precise geometric formations.
In the early 1930s Berkeley presented elaborately staged dance sequences within well-worn stories, in films such as 42nd Street (1933).
By the mid-1930s, singing and dancing teams such as Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers had overtaken Berkeley's spectacles in popularity.
Fred Astaire simplified the movie musical: dancers were shot in full figure, with a minimum of edits and camera angles.

title: Screwball comedy's sparring couples
description: Screwball comedies of the 1930s and 1940s paired seemingly mismatched lovers in zany situations and rapid, overlapping dialogue; It Happened One Night helped set the pattern.

facts.text: It Happened One Night (1934), Frank Capra's comedy about a runaway heiress and a reporter, was the first film to win all five major Academy Awards and helped establish screwball conventions.
Screwball conventions include seemingly mismatched lovers in unlikely romances, off-the-wall characters and zany situations.
Screwball comedies often showed elegantly dressed couples in opulent Art Deco settings whose shared mischief proved them suited as lovers.
In Bringing Up Baby (1938), Katharine Hepburn's eccentric heiress pursues Cary Grant's bookish paleontologist through a series of farcical mishaps.
Howard Hawks made overlapping dialogue a trademark, and His Girl Friday (1940) is known for its rapid-fire delivery.
For His Girl Friday, Hawks changed The Front Page's newspaper editor and reporter from two men to a man (Cary Grant) and a woman (Rosalind Russell).

title: Why screwball couples spar
description: Depression-era studios wanted stories of people beating adversity, and the Hays Code banned explicit sexual references, so verbal sparring and physical comedy stood in for sex.

facts.text: During the Depression, with film attendance in decline, studios sought audiences with stories that showed protagonists triumphing over adversity.
The Hays Code, Hollywood's own guidelines from 1934 to 1968, banned explicit mention of sexual relationships, so verbal sparring and physical comedy took the place of sexuality.

title: Why people choose to be scared
description: Horror aims to cause fear or dread; a 2020 haunted-house study found enjoyment peaks at a just-right amount of fear, which researchers liken to play.

facts.text: Britannica defines a horror film as one calculated to cause intense repugnance, fear or dread.
In a 2020 study, researchers fitted 110 visitors to a commercial haunted house in Vejle, Denmark, with heart rate monitors.
Recreational fear is the mixed experience of feeling fear and enjoyment at the same time.
Enjoyment followed an inverted U: visitors who were barely scared or too scared enjoyed the haunted house less than those at a just-right level of fear.
The researchers compare recreational fear to play: enjoyment comes from just-right departures from a person's normal physiological state.

title: Horror by suggestion: Cat People
description: Val Lewton's Cat People (1942) never shows its monster; shadows, low light and long silences let the viewer's imagination build the dread.

facts.text: Cat People (1942), produced by Val Lewton for RKO, never shows its heroine Irena in cat form and relies on suggestion and the viewer's imagination.
Britannica notes Cat People for its masterful use of shadows and low lighting to create suspense.
Lewton worked on skeletal budgets, and his films often hold silence for long periods to build dread.

title: Film noir's dark look
description: French critics named American crime films of the 1940s film noir; their signature is stark high-contrast lighting that isolates the hero, with roots in German Expressionism.

facts.text: French critics coined the term film noir, meaning dark film, after World War II, admiring American crime films for their cynical characters and dark, brooding style.
Banned in occupied countries during the war, these American films became available throughout Europe beginning in 1946.
Stark high-contrast lighting, film noir's most notable visual feature, underscores the isolation of the typical noir hero.
Film noir's shadowy style traces back to German Expressionist films such as The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (1920).
Typical noir images include rain-soaked streets and flashing neon signs.

title: Why film noir flourished in the 1940s
description: Noir drew stories from hard-boiled crime novels, reflected postwar disillusionment, and attracted European-born directors who felt like outsiders in Hollywood.

facts.text: The Maltese Falcon (1941), John Huston's first film as director, adapted Dashiell Hammett's 1930 hard-boiled detective novel and is considered by some the first major work of noir.
Double Indemnity (1944), directed by Billy Wilder, adapted a novel by James M. Cain, with Raymond Chandler as co-writer.
Britannica links film noir to postwar disillusionment: an unstable peacetime economy, McCarthyism and the looming threat of atomic warfare.
European-born directors such as Billy Wilder and Fritz Lang, trained to stress style, often felt like outsiders in the Hollywood studio system and were drawn to noir.

title: 1950s science fiction and the atom
description: 1950s science fiction turned atomic-age fear into story: a visitor warns Earth about its bombs, and bomb tests breed giant ants.

facts.text: In The Day the Earth Stood Still (1951), directed by Robert Wise, the visitor Klaatu lands in Washington, D.C., and warns that humanity's atomic weapons threaten other civilizations.
Britannica calls The Day the Earth Stood Still a classic that reflects the fears of the Cold War and the early atomic age.
In Them! (1954), directed by Gordon Douglas, giant ants mutated by atomic bomb tests in the New Mexico desert threaten humanity.
Britannica calls Them! arguably the best of the 1950s giant atomic-mutant creature movies.

title: Invasion stories as mirrors of their time
description: Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1956) shows pod people replacing humans; made at the height of the Cold War, it has been read as an allegory of many fears, though its director denied any political intent.

facts.text: In Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1956), directed by Don Siegel, aliens grow in seedpods and take over people's bodies while they sleep, leaving duplicates without human emotion.
Made at the height of the Cold War, the film has been read as an allegory of Cold War paranoia, fear of McCarthyism, alienation in mass society or loss of autonomy under communism.
Siegel dismissed such readings and said he did not intend a political message.

title: Hitchcock's bomb: surprise versus suspense
description: Hitchcock contrasted a bomb that explodes without warning (15 seconds of surprise) with one the audience knows about (15 minutes of suspense), because the informed audience participates.

facts.text: In 1962 François Truffaut interviewed Alfred Hitchcock at length; the resulting book, Le Cinéma selon Alfred Hitchcock, was published in 1966.
In Hitchcock's example, a bomb under a table explodes without warning during an ordinary chat, giving the audience 15 seconds of surprise.
If the audience sees the bomb planted, knows it will explode at one o'clock and sees a clock at a quarter to one, the same scene gives 15 minutes of suspense.
Hitchcock said the harmless conversation becomes fascinating because the audience is participating in the scene.

title: Suspense by telling: Double Indemnity
description: A film can build a whole story on what the audience already knows: Double Indemnity reveals who committed the crime at the start, trading a mystery for suspense.

facts.text: Double Indemnity lets the audience know who committed the crime from the start, making it a character-driven drama rather than a mystery.

title: Parody: a genre's rules played for laughs
description: Parodies such as Blazing Saddles and Young Frankenstein (both 1974) imitate a genre's conventions and look closely enough for audiences to recognize them, then play them for laughs.

facts.text: Blazing Saddles (1974), directed by Mel Brooks, spoofs westerns with a Black sheriff at its center, satirizing racial prejudice and western conventions.
Young Frankenstein (1974), also by Mel Brooks, parodies Universal's Frankenstein films; its black-and-white cinematography replicated the look of Bride of Frankenstein (1935).

title: Revisionist films turn a genre's rules around
description: Acclaimed films often invoke a genre's conventions only to break them; revisionist Westerns such as Unforgiven (1992) turned the genre's codes against themselves.

facts.text: Britannica notes that often the most acclaimed films invoke a genre's conventions only to break them down.
Britannica traces the western from Stagecoach to Unforgiven (1992), which it describes as an ironic perversion of the genre's codes.
Unforgiven, a revisionist western, took an unsentimental look at frontier violence and won Academy Awards for best picture and best director.

title: Where one genre ends: setting, subject or style
description: Most genres are defined by subject or setting, but the musical can be about almost anything, and film noir is often called a style that crosses genres rather than a genre.

facts.text: Britannica calls film noir a stylistic approach rather than a distinct genre, and notes debate over whether it is a genre or a style common to many genres.
The noir label applies mostly to crime dramas, but some critics cite certain westerns and comedies as film noir.
The musical often has a show-business setting, but it is not so narrowly restricted and can be about almost any subject.
